extracted.intended_audience: newsroom product people, journalists, media-industry observers, and digital-news strategists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical observations for designing, launching, and judging mobile news apps that use chat or conversational interfaces — what tends to work, fail, and why. Focused on product/editorial/distribution trade-offs for news publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive product/value beyond headline lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers' native news apps have mostly been 'boring' — just lists of headlines you can tap — and successful apps need distinctive forms or formats rather than a simple headline list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of distinctive approaches include NYT Now (aggregated stories), The Economist’s Espresso (summaries), BuzzFeed News app (newsletter-like + push creativity), Reuters TV (auto-packaged video shows). Anti-pattern: shipping a basic headline list and calling it an 'app' without a clear unique value proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chat UI risks an 'uncanny valley' — clarify who/what the user is interacting with
rubrics_metrics.description: A chat interface immediately raises the question: 'Am I talking with a bot? A person? A news organization?' That textual uncanny valley can confuse users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice is to make the model clear (e.g., scripted responses written by staff but delivered by software). Anti-patterns: interfaces that leave users unsure whether replies are human or automated, which undermines trust or utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Users generally don't want news injected into personal chat spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Chat apps are 'walled-off spaces for personal communications' and users tend not to welcome news organizations pushing content into those private arenas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating friends' chat environments as a default distribution channel for broad news push; consider opt-in, tightly targeted, or niche use cases. Evidence cited: low user engagement and critiques like 'Does anyone really want news flooding their Messenger?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform selection and platform constraints matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Different messaging platforms have different rules and affordances (e.g., WhatsApp limited broadcast to groups >256 and considered banning newsletter distribution), which constrain publishers' ability to reach audiences via chat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design distribution strategies around platform policies and limits. Anti-pattern: assuming all messengers are equally usable for publisher push without checking restrictions or long-term platform intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational/news-chat formats are likely to work best in specific niches
rubrics_metrics.description: Chat interfaces and conversational journalism experiments will 'work best in specific niches' rather than as a broad, general-purpose replacement for mainstream news distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target narrow use-cases where conversational style adds clear value (e.g., highly personalized briefings, localized alerts, specialized verticals). Broad general-audience push is less likely to scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with existing editorial/news flows is challenging
rubrics_metrics.description: Chat-driven formats are 'a challenge to integrate into existing news flows' and require editorial workflows and staffing different from standard publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for staffing, scripting, and operational changes; consider cost and complexity to avoid operational mismatch. Anti-pattern: bolting chat UI onto existing workflows without process redesign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between personal (expensive) and bot-driven (cheap but poor) approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Products must find the 'right balance between personal-but-expensive-to-run and bot-driven-but-not-all-that-good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sustainability: highly personalized conversational experiences can be costly to produce at scale; fully automated bots can feel hollow. Hybrid models with scripted human-authored content delivered by automation may be an option, but evaluate trade-offs carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand must guide product and editorial vision
rubrics_metrics.description: The product form should express and be driven by the core editorial mission and brand — e.g., 'our brand... is the most important thing' that drives editorial mission, product vision, and business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure new formats are coherent with the publisher's brand promise and audience expectations. Anti-pattern: launching formats that conflict with or dilute core brand identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize friction between readers and content (API philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy exemplified by 'Quartz is an API' and 'put as little friction as possible between us and our readers' — design products to let content go where readers are in an appropriate form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use APIs and modular content to adapt formats to platforms; focus on reducing barriers to access while maintaining editorial standards. Score products by how little friction they impose for users to reach content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure viability by real user adoption and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: App success should be judged by audience traction (e.g., Quartz Brief averaged 23,000 downloads a month and still wasn't considered large enough).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track downloads, active users, retention, engagement; be realistic about what counts as 'scale' for sustainability. Anti-pattern: relying solely on industry admiration or press attention rather than hard user metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational scripting must encourage engagement and feel human
rubrics_metrics.description: In Quartz's case, staff condensed stories into scripts of back-and-forth responses that 'encouraged engagement with the story and felt human.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest editorial craft in scripting conversational flows; avoid dry or purely headline-driven bot messages. Example practice: human-written scripts sent programmatically to preserve voice while scaling distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: User experience must avoid feeling like 'glorified push notifications' or a chore
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques noted that some news chatbots become 'basically... glorified push notifications' and 'it quickly became a chore to even look at them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design frequency, relevance, and interaction patterns to avoid overload; prioritize meaningful, contextual interactions over volume-driven pushes. Anti-pattern: high-frequency, low-value messages that mimic spam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments are valuable but subject to external business and ownership changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Product experiments' fate can be influenced by acquisition, corporate strategy shifts, paywalls, and resource allocation (e.g., Quartz's acquisition by Uzabase and subsequent app changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or planning experiments, factor in organizational stability and long-term support; success requires both user adoption and ongoing institutional commitment.
